newsitem.title: UK: MINOR METALS - Quiet, activity to pick up soon.
newsitem.headline: MINOR METALS - Quiet, activity to pick up soon.

text.p: Business in minor metals remained slow during the week but was punctuated by brief flurries of consumer buying ahead of the traditionally brisk fourth quarter.
"Its been quiet, though demand is picking up," a trader said.
Cobalt firmed against a backdrop of tight supplies, while a recent Ukrainian germanium metal tender continued to baffle market operators.
Elsewhere prices held steady levels.
Demand for cobalt lifted Russian and high grade material.

The Gorham/Intertech cobalt conference which finished on Wednesday had scant impact on the uptrending market. But traders said it raised some potentially bearish issues such as a forecast by industry analysts Roskill that cobalt, against the backdrop of increased global production, could fall to $10 per lb by the year 2000.

Roskill said world production could rise to 50,000 tonnes a year, with demand at 30,000 at best. Also, Michael Garvey, president of Garvey Associates said cobalt was moving towards oversupply by the end of the decade and prices were set to drop. But several London traders were not fully convinced.

They said some planned production hikes may not materialise. "Fifty percent of new production could fall by the wayside, while demand is expected to grow," one said. "The year 2,000 is a long way off...I was slightly disappointed the conference did not tackle supply/demand figures for 1997/98 which is potentially a boom period," he added. Near-term prices for both Russian and high grade material are set to rise by around $2 over current levels. One trader suggested high grade material could reach $30 by 1997, with Russian running close behind at $28.
Tightness of better grades saw some users divert to poor quality residue and scrap material, a sign of short supply.
Falconbridge, who produce eight million lbs a year of very high cobalt, are underselling the metal and losing potential revenue of some $35 million, one trader suggested.

Their cobalt, in tight supply anyway, is 99.9 percent purity, tailor-made for the high-tech aerospace turbine super alloy market, and could easily go for a $2/$3 premium over current high-grade prices.
Because they sell their cobalt at levels close to the 99.3 percent high grade price, they are preventing the other grades, such as Russian, from moving up as fundamentals dictate.
In germanium, market talk focused on the recent Ukrainian tender which left Western traders pondering its next move.
"I am sure the deal for the Ukraine material has now concluded...there has been talk that transportation arrangments have been made," a trader said.

But another said, "The deal was not completed as prices were falling before the tender and the original buyers at the higher levels backed off," another said. In any event nearly all traders agreed that the exact terms of the deal would be slow to emerge.

At the moment prices are adopting a downside bias, though underlying demand was likely to emerge soon. "Consumers are living off their last ounce of stock hoping prices will fall further," one trader commented.
Another noted that Russian stockpiled material may be tendered in 1997, but this is taking a back seat at present.

Pricewise antimony remained elusive as bears and bulls again failed to agree. Some suggested that a plentiful supply of Chinese metal was capping the market, adding that consumers were not buying in anticipation of lower prices.
Rebuffing the Chinese factor one trader said, "The Chinese material has been of poor quality, arriving with ten times the amount of the normal tin content."

Antimony stocks hold reasonable levels but could quickly be eaten away if expected fourth quarter demand hits the market. Talk of a meeting between Chinese producers helped to firm manganese. Upcoming long term consumer contracts underpinned magnesium. Japanese interest was noted in iridium and indium, though so far they have not yet covered. Both have the potential to head higher near-term, traders said.
